title: Async File Upload & Processing Pipeline
description: A SaaS platform lets users upload large files — CSVs, PDFs, images — which then get processed: virus scanned, parsed, thumbnail generated, and stored. Navigate the five hardest design decisions in building this reliably at scale.
overview:
DocFlow is a B2B document management SaaS platform built on ASP.NET Web API (.NET 8), hosted on Azure App Service. HR departments, legal teams, and finance divisions at enterprise companies use DocFlow to upload, process, and manage business-critical documents — employment contracts, payslips, compliance certificates, and financial reports.

At peak, DocFlow receives 3,000 file uploads per hour across 180 enterprise tenants. Files range from small PDFs (50KB) to large CSV exports (500MB). Every uploaded file travels through a four-step processing pipeline before it is available to the user:

1. Virus Scan — the file is scanned for malware and malicious content before any other processing begins.
2. Content Parsing — structured data is extracted from the file: text from PDFs, rows from CSVs, metadata from images.
3. Thumbnail Generation — a preview image is generated for supported file types and stored alongside the original.
4. Indexing — extracted content is indexed for full-text search so users can find documents by content, not just filename.

The platform's infrastructure consists of Azure Blob Storage for raw file storage; Azure Service Bus for async job messaging between the API and worker services; Azure SQL for job status tracking, file metadata, and extracted content; Azure Cache for Redis for idempotency locks and job deduplication; and Application Insights for end-to-end telemetry and alerting.

Right now, the platform has several critical design gaps — files travel through the API server, processing is synchronous, duplicate uploads cause corrupted records, infected files are not handled safely, and stuck processing jobs go undetected for hours.

steps.interviewerSays: DocFlow needs to let users upload files up to 500MB — CSVs, PDFs, and images. Your first instinct might be to accept the file in a POST request to your API, save it, and return a success response. Why might that be a problem at scale, and how would you redesign the upload flow?
steps.context: This tests whether the engineer understands why large file uploads should never go through the API server. The correct answer introduces presigned URLs — a pattern used by AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, and every major storage provider. Many 3-5 year engineers have used this pattern but cannot explain why it exists.

options.text: Large files slow the API response time, so we should increase the request timeout to 5 minutes and stream the file through the API server to blob storage — this handles 500MB transfers without changing the upload flow
options.interviewerReaction: Increasing timeouts treats the symptom not the cause. Every concurrent upload still holds an open connection, consumes memory, and routes all bytes through your server — with 100 simultaneous uploads you are holding 50GB in flight through your API tier. What if your server was not involved in the file transfer at all?

options.text: Streaming 500MB through the API server holds connections open, consumes memory, and does not scale — instead the API should generate a short-lived presigned URL and return it to the client, who uploads directly to Azure Blob Storage, keeping every file byte completely out of the API server
options.interviewerReaction: Exactly right — you identified the problem and the solution together. The API issues a signed permission token and steps aside entirely. Now the file is in blob storage — how do you trigger and track the processing pipeline that needs to run on it?

options.text: The API POST approach has memory problems at 500MB, so we should chunk the file on the client into 10MB pieces and POST each chunk separately to the API — this reduces per-request memory pressure and lets us reassemble on the server
options.interviewerReaction: Chunking reduces per-request memory pressure but your API server still handles every byte of every chunk from every concurrent upload. With 100 simultaneous uploads you are still routing 50GB through your API tier — just in smaller pieces. The server is still the bottleneck. What if no chunks went through your server at all?

idealAnswer.summary: Large file uploads must never travel through your API server. Presigned URLs delegate the upload directly from the client to blob storage — your API server issues a signed permission token and steps aside. This eliminates connection holding, memory pressure, and network egress costs from your API tier entirely.

sections.heading: Why Streaming Through Your API Server Fails at Scale
sections.content:
When a 500MB file upload travels through your API server, three things happen simultaneously:

1. One HTTP connection is held open for the entire upload duration — potentially minutes on a slow connection. With 100 concurrent uploads, that is 100 long-held connections consuming threads or async handlers.

2. The file bytes pass through your server's memory, even when streaming. At scale this creates memory pressure that competes with your actual application logic.

3. Your server pays network ingress and egress costs twice — once receiving from the client, once sending to blob storage.

Presigned URLs solve all three by removing your server from the data path entirely. Your server only handles the lightweight token issuance — a millisecond operation — while the heavy file transfer happens directly between the client and Azure Blob Storage over a connection your server never touches.

sections.heading: Presigned URL Upload Flow
sections.content:
WRONG WAY (file travels through API)
  ──────────────────────────────────────
  Client ──500MB──► API Server ──500MB──► Blob Storage
                    (bottleneck)

  RIGHT WAY (presigned URL)
  ──────────────────────────────────────

  STEP 1 — Client requests upload permission
  Client ──POST /files/upload-url──► API Server
  Body: { filename: 'report.csv', size: 524288000 }

  STEP 2 — API generates presigned URL
  API Server:
  → Validate user is authenticated
  → Validate file type is allowed
  → Validate file size is within limit
  → Generate unique file ID: uuid-1234
  → Create pending record in DB:
    { id: uuid-1234, status: PENDING_UPLOAD,
      userId: u-99, filename: report.csv }
  → Call Azure Blob Storage SDK:
    Generate SAS URL for blob: uploads/uuid-1234
    Expiry: 15 minutes
    Permissions: write only
  → Return to client:
    { fileId: uuid-1234,
      uploadUrl: https://storage.blob.core.windows.net/
                 uploads/uuid-1234?sv=...&sig=...&se=...,
      expiresAt: 2024-03-10T14:45:00Z }

  STEP 3 — Client uploads directly to blob storage
  Client ──500MB──► Azure Blob Storage
  (API server not involved — zero bytes through API)

  STEP 4 — Client notifies API that upload is complete
  Client ──POST /files/uuid-1234/complete──► API Server
  → API updates DB: status: UPLOADED
  → API triggers processing pipeline
  → API returns: { fileId: uuid-1234,
                   status: PROCESSING }

sections.heading: Key Principles
items: Presigned URL expiry should match expected upload time plus a buffer — 15 minutes for a 500MB file on a slow connection is reasonable
Permissions on the presigned URL must be write-only — the client should not be able to read other users' uploads from the same URL pattern
Create the pending DB record before issuing the URL — if the client never completes the upload, you have a record to clean up with a scheduled job
Validate file type and size at URL generation time, not just at processing time — reject disallowed file types before the client wastes time uploading 500MB
Blob storage path should include the fileId, not the original filename — original filenames are user input and must never be used directly as storage paths

sections.heading: The Completion Notification Gap
sections.content:
A common mistake is relying solely on the client calling POST /files/{id}/complete to trigger processing. If the client crashes, closes the browser, or loses connectivity after the upload completes but before sending the completion notification, your system has a file sitting in blob storage with status: PENDING_UPLOAD forever.

The fix: configure an Azure Blob Storage event trigger — when a blob is written to the uploads container, Azure Event Grid automatically fires an event to your API. Use this as the authoritative completion signal, with the client notification as a fast-path optimisation. Never rely on client-side callbacks as the only trigger for server-side state transitions.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
pros: API server is completely out of the data path — no memory pressure, no connection holding, no egress costs
Azure Blob Storage handles upload reliability natively — resumable uploads, automatic retry on network interruption
Scales to thousands of concurrent uploads without any API server scaling
Write-only presigned URL means a leaked URL cannot be used to read other data
cons: Two-step flow (get URL, then notify completion) adds client-side complexity compared to a simple POST
Presigned URL expiry must be tuned carefully — too short and slow connections fail, too long and a stolen URL is valid longer than acceptable
Client completion notification is unreliable — requires blob storage event trigger as a safety net

idealAnswer.oneLineSummary: Large file uploads should never travel through your API server — presigned URLs let clients upload directly to blob storage while your API only handles the lightweight permission issuance.

steps.interviewerSays: Good. The file is now in blob storage. We need to run three processing steps on it: a virus scan, content parsing to extract structured data, and thumbnail generation for image files. Each step takes between 5 and 90 seconds. How do you design the processing pipeline, and how does the user know what is happening with their file?
steps.context: This tests whether the engineer understands why long-running work must be async, how to model job status, and how to communicate progress back to the user without polling hammering the server. Many mid-level engineers make the processing synchronous and wonder why their API times out.

options.text: Run all three processing steps synchronously in the API request thread when the completion notification arrives — return the result when all steps finish
options.interviewerReaction: A 90-second synchronous operation in an API request will hit HTTP timeout limits, consume a thread for the entire duration, and give the user no feedback during processing. If the server restarts mid-processing, the work is lost entirely. How do you move this work outside the request thread?

options.text: On completion notification, publish a message to a queue, return 202 Accepted to the client immediately, have background worker pods consume the queue and process the file, update a status record in the database after each step, and let the client poll GET /files/{id}/status to track progress
options.interviewerReaction: Exactly right. Async queue decouples upload from processing, 202 gives the user immediate feedback, and status polling keeps them informed without blocking the API. One follow-up — what happens if the virus scan fails? Does content parsing still run?

options.text: Run the processing in a background thread on the API server using Task.Run, update the database when complete, and send the user an email notification when processing finishes
options.interviewerReaction: Background threads on the API server are lost if the pod restarts — you have no durability guarantee. If processing takes 90 seconds and the pod is redeployed mid-processing, the work silently disappears. How do you make the processing durable and survivable across pod restarts?

idealAnswer.summary: Long-running file processing must be fully asynchronous — decoupled from the API request, durable across pod restarts, and observable through a status model. A message queue with dedicated worker pods is the correct architecture. The API returns 202 Accepted immediately and the client polls for status updates.

sections.heading: Why Async Processing is Non-Negotiable Here
sections.content:
Processing a 500MB file involves three operations totalling up to 90 seconds. Running this synchronously creates three compounding problems:

1. HTTP timeout: most clients and load balancers timeout at 30-60 seconds. A 90-second operation will be killed mid-way.

2. Thread starvation: each synchronous processing job holds a thread on your API server. With 50 concurrent uploads all processing simultaneously, your API server is unresponsive to every other request.

3. No durability: if the server restarts during processing — deployment, crash, scaling event — the work is silently lost with no way to recover.

The solution is to treat file processing as a job, not a request. The API acknowledges receipt immediately (202 Accepted) and hands the work to a durable queue. Worker pods consume jobs independently and update status as they progress.

sections.heading: Async Processing Pipeline
sections.content:
Blob Storage event fires: file uploaded
               │
               ▼
         API Server
         → Update DB: status: QUEUED
         → Publish to Service Bus:
           { fileId: uuid-1234,
             userId: u-99,
             blobPath: uploads/uuid-1234,
             steps: [VIRUS_SCAN,
                     CONTENT_PARSE,
                     THUMBNAIL_GEN] }
         → Return 202 to client (if via client notify)
               │
               ▼
      Azure Service Bus Queue
      file-processing-jobs
               │
               ▼
       Worker Pod (auto-scaling)
               │
    ┌──────────▼──────────────────────┐
    │  STEP 1: VIRUS SCAN             │
    │  → Update DB: status: SCANNING  │
    │  → Run virus scan               │
    │  → Clean: proceed to step 2     │
    │  → Infected: update status:     │
    │    REJECTED, delete blob,       │
    │    notify user, STOP            │
    └──────────┬──────────────────────┘
               │ clean
    ┌──────────▼──────────────────────┐
    │  STEP 2: CONTENT PARSING        │
    │  → Update DB: status: PARSING   │
    │  → Parse CSV/PDF structure      │
    │  → Store extracted data in DB   │
    │  → Update DB: status: PARSED    │
    └──────────┬──────────────────────┘
               │
    ┌──────────▼──────────────────────┐
    │  STEP 3: THUMBNAIL GENERATION   │
    │  → Update DB: status: PROCESSING│
    │  → Generate thumbnail if image  │
    │  → Upload thumbnail to blob     │
    │  → Update DB: status: COMPLETE, │
    │    thumbnailUrl: ...,           │
    │    processedAt: timestamp       │
    └─────────────────────────────────┘

  CLIENT POLLING:
  GET /files/uuid-1234/status
  Response:
  {
    fileId: uuid-1234,
    status: PARSING,        ← current step
    progress: 40,           ← percent complete
    steps: [
      { name: VIRUS_SCAN,   state: COMPLETE },
      { name: CONTENT_PARSE,state: IN_PROGRESS },
      { name: THUMBNAIL_GEN,state: PENDING }
    ],
    startedAt: ...,
    estimatedCompletion: ...
  }

sections.heading: Key Principles
items: Return 202 Accepted immediately — never make the user wait for async work to complete before acknowledging their request
Update the status record in the DB before starting each step, not after — if the worker crashes mid-step, the status accurately reflects where processing stopped
Virus scan must always be the first step — never parse or store content from an unscanned file
Worker pods must be stateless — all state lives in the DB and blob storage, so any pod can pick up any job
Set a message lock timeout on Service Bus equal to the maximum expected processing time — if a worker crashes, the message becomes visible again and another pod picks it up automatically

sections.heading: The Polling Frequency Trap
sections.content:
If the client polls GET /files/{id}/status every second for a 90-second job, that is 90 API calls per file per user. With 1,000 concurrent uploads in progress, that is 1,000 status calls per second — a significant load generated entirely by waiting, not by actual user actions.

Three ways to manage this: exponential backoff polling (poll at 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s intervals), a maximum poll interval cap of 5 seconds, or replacing polling entirely with a WebSocket or Server-Sent Events connection that pushes status updates to the client as they happen. For a 3-5 year engineer, polling with exponential backoff is the right answer. WebSocket push is the senior optimisation.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
pros: Processing is durable — a pod restart or deployment during processing does not lose work, the message is requeued automatically
Worker pods scale independently of the API — burst upload periods scale workers without scaling the API tier
Step-by-step status gives users meaningful progress feedback, not just a spinner
Virus scan failure path is clean — infected files are rejected and deleted before any content is parsed or stored
cons: More moving parts than synchronous processing — Service Bus, worker pods, and status DB all need to be operational
Client must implement polling logic — adds frontend complexity
Processing order dependencies (virus scan before parse) must be explicitly enforced — a queue does not know about step ordering

idealAnswer.oneLineSummary: Any operation taking more than a few seconds belongs in an async queue with a status model — never hold an HTTP connection open for work that could survive a pod restart.

steps.interviewerSays: Good pipeline design. Now a reliability problem. A user uploads the same CSV file twice — maybe they got impatient and clicked upload again, or their client retried after a network hiccup. Your worker picks up both processing jobs and runs them concurrently. What problems does this cause, and how do you design the system to handle duplicate processing safely?
steps.context: This is the idempotency problem. It is one of the most important concepts in distributed systems and one of the least understood by mid-level engineers. They know what idempotency means in HTTP (GET is idempotent, POST is not) but most have never had to design for it in a processing pipeline.

options.text: Add a unique constraint on the filename in the database — if the same filename is uploaded twice, reject the second upload with a 409 Conflict error
options.interviewerReaction: Filename uniqueness is too restrictive — users legitimately upload files with the same name, like a monthly report called 'summary.csv'. And this does not solve the case where the same file bytes are uploaded twice under different names. How do you detect true duplicates — same content — rather than same filename?

options.text: The problem is that filename is not a reliable identity for file content — two uploads of identical bytes under different names will both process. The fix is to hash the file bytes to get a content fingerprint, check for an existing processed result with that hash, and if found skip processing entirely and link the new upload to the existing result
options.interviewerReaction: Exactly right — you named the real problem first, which is that filename uniqueness is the wrong identity for duplicate detection, then gave the correct solution. How do you handle the race condition where two workers compute the same hash at exactly the same moment and both try to claim processing?

options.text: Let both jobs process concurrently — the second one to complete will overwrite the first result in the database. Use the latest result as the canonical processed output
options.interviewerReaction: Last-write-wins creates a race condition where two workers are simultaneously writing results to the database, partially overwriting each other's output. The final state is unpredictable and potentially corrupt. How do you prevent two workers from processing the same file at the same time?

idealAnswer.summary: Duplicate file processing is solved with two complementary mechanisms: a content hash that detects identical files regardless of filename, and an optimistic lock or database unique constraint on the processing job that prevents two workers from processing the same content simultaneously. Together these make the processing pipeline idempotent.

sections.heading: What Idempotency Means in a Processing Pipeline
sections.content:
An idempotent operation produces the same result whether it runs once or ten times. In a file processing pipeline, idempotency means: processing the same file content twice should produce exactly the same output as processing it once — and should not create duplicate records, duplicate thumbnails, or duplicate extracted data.

This matters because in distributed systems, duplicate processing is not an edge case — it is a normal operating condition. Networks drop connections. Clients retry. Message queues redeliver messages when workers crash. A processing pipeline that cannot handle duplicates safely will corrupt data in production eventually.

sections.heading: Idempotent Processing Design
sections.content:
FILE UPLOAD COMPLETE
               │
               ▼
  STEP 1: GENERATE CONTENT HASH
  Worker downloads file from blob storage
  Computes SHA-256 hash of file bytes
  contentHash: a3f8c2d1...
               │
               ▼
  STEP 2: CHECK FOR EXISTING RESULT
  SELECT * FROM processed_files
  WHERE contentHash = 'a3f8c2d1...'
  AND userId = 'u-99'
               │
        ┌──────┴──────┐
        │ FOUND       │ NOT FOUND
        ▼             ▼
  Link new      Attempt to claim
  upload record  processing lock:
  to existing   ─────────────────
  result.        INSERT INTO
  Skip           processing_locks
  processing.    (contentHash,
  Status:        workerId,
  COMPLETE       lockedAt)
  immediately.   WHERE NOT EXISTS
                 (same contentHash)
                    │
             ┌──────┴──────┐
             │ LOCK WON    │ LOCK LOST
             ▼             ▼
        Process        Another worker
        the file       has the lock.
        normally.      Poll until
             │         complete,
             ▼         then link
        Release        to their
        lock.          result.
        Store result
        with contentHash.

  DATABASE SCHEMA ADDITIONS:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  file_uploads                       │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────  │
  │  id            UUID PRIMARY KEY     │
  │  userId        UUID                 │
  │  filename      VARCHAR              │
  │  contentHash   VARCHAR(64)          │  ← SHA-256
  │  status        ENUM                 │
  │  resultId      UUID NULLABLE        │  ← links to result
  │                                     │
  │  processing_locks                   │
  │  ─────────────────────────────────  │
  │  contentHash   VARCHAR UNIQUE       │  ← prevents race
  │  workerId      VARCHAR              │
  │  lockedAt      DATETIME             │
  │  expiresAt     DATETIME             │  ← stale lock cleanup
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

sections.heading: Key Principles
items: Use SHA-256 for content hashing — fast enough for files up to 500MB and collision-resistant for practical purposes
Hash the file bytes, not the filename — same content with different filename is still a duplicate
The UNIQUE constraint on processing_locks.contentHash is your race condition protection — the database enforces that only one worker can claim a lock, not application code
Processing locks must have an expiry time — if the worker that claimed the lock crashes, the lock must expire and become available for another worker after a reasonable timeout
Scope duplicate detection to the user — user A and user B uploading the same file should process independently, not share results across account boundaries

sections.heading: Do Not Hash Inside the API Request
sections.content:
A common mistake is computing the content hash in the API server when the completion notification arrives — before queueing the processing job. This requires downloading the file from blob storage into the API server just to hash it, which reintroduces the same memory and network problems that presigned URLs solved.

The correct place to compute the hash is inside the worker, as the first step of processing — the worker is already downloading the file to process it, so hashing happens as part of the same read pass. No extra download, no extra memory pressure on the API tier.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
pros: Content hashing detects true duplicates regardless of filename, upload time, or which client submitted them
Database-level unique constraint on the lock prevents race conditions without distributed locking infrastructure
Duplicate uploads complete instantly for the second requester — they get the result from the first processing run immediately
Lock expiry prevents stale locks from blocking processing permanently after worker failures
cons: SHA-256 hashing a 500MB file adds processing time — typically 1-3 seconds on modern hardware, acceptable as the first step of a 90-second pipeline
Sharing results across duplicate uploads requires careful data modelling — the result record must be associated with the user, not just the hash
Lock expiry timeout must be tuned carefully — too short and you get spurious re-processing, too long and crashed workers block processing for an unacceptable time

idealAnswer.oneLineSummary: Idempotency in a processing pipeline means the same input always produces the same output regardless of how many times it runs — content hashing detects duplicates and database-level locks prevent concurrent processing of identical content.

steps.interviewerSays: The pipeline is running. At 11am, your virus scanner flags an uploaded file — a PDF submitted by a finance user at one of DocFlow's enterprise tenants. The scan result is: INFECTED. The file contains a known macro exploit. What exactly happens now — walk me through every action the system must take, in order, and explain why the sequence matters.
steps.context: This tests security thinking and fail-fast pipeline design. The wrong answers either continue processing the infected file, notify the user too late, or leave traces of the infected content in the system. The right answer is a precise, ordered shutdown of that file's lifecycle with no data leakage between steps.

options.text: Log the virus scan result, mark the file status as INFECTED in the database, and notify the user by email — the file stays in blob storage in case the security team needs to investigate it later
options.interviewerReaction: Keeping an infected file in blob storage — even flagged — is a liability. Any misconfigured access policy, any storage key leak, any future bug in your access control layer could expose that file to another user or another service. An infected file has no legitimate use case in your storage — it must be deleted. What is the complete sequence of actions, starting from the scan result and ending with the file entirely gone from your infrastructure?

options.text: In strict order: immediately delete the infected blob from Azure Blob Storage so no other process or user can access it, update the file record status to REJECTED with the scan result and timestamp, complete the Service Bus message to stop any redelivery, send a notification to the uploading user explaining the file was rejected and why, and log a security event to Application Insights with the tenant ID, user ID, file hash, and scanner verdict for audit purposes — content parsing and thumbnail generation must never run
options.interviewerReaction: Exactly right — and the sequence you described is critical. Delete first, then update status, then notify. If you notify the user before deleting the blob, there is a window where the user knows the file exists and the file is still accessible. Delete makes the file unreachable before any other action. The audit log is also important — a security team needs to know this happened, when, and from which tenant. How do you make sure the virus scanner result itself cannot be tampered with or bypassed by a malicious file?

options.text: Mark the file as QUARANTINED, move it to a separate restricted blob container accessible only to the security team, pause processing and alert the security team to manually review the file before deciding whether to proceed or delete it
options.interviewerReaction: Quarantine containers sound thorough but introduce unnecessary risk and operational overhead. You now maintain a container of live malicious files that requires strict access control, regular review, and a manual process to clear. If that container is ever misconfigured — even briefly — you have a breach. For a document management SaaS, there is no legitimate reason to retain an infected file. The correct posture is immediate deletion. Quarantine is appropriate for security research environments, not production SaaS platforms.

idealAnswer.summary: An infected file must be deleted from storage before any other action — not flagged, not quarantined, deleted. The sequence is: delete blob, update status, stop pipeline, notify user, write audit log. The order matters because every action before deletion is a window where the infected file is still reachable.

sections.heading: Why Sequence Matters in Security Response
sections.content:
When a virus scan returns INFECTED, the first instinct is often to update the database and then clean up. This gets the sequence backwards. Every millisecond between the scan result and the blob deletion is a window where the infected file exists in your storage with a known path.

If your notification goes out before the delete, the user has a URL window. If your status update fires an event before the delete, a misconfigured event subscriber could attempt to process the file. If the worker crashes between status update and delete, the file is flagged in the DB but still physically present in storage.

Delete first. Everything else is commentary.

sections.heading: Infected File Response — Exact Sequence
sections.content:
Virus Scanner returns: INFECTED
  Threat: macro exploit, PDF
               │
               ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ACTION 1: DELETE BLOB (first, always)  │
  │  Azure Blob Storage SDK:                │
  │  blobClient.DeleteAsync(               │
  │    uploads/uuid-1234)                   │
  │  File is now unreachable by anyone      │
  └──────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                 │
  ┌──────────────▼──────────────────────────┐
  │  ACTION 2: UPDATE DATABASE STATUS       │
  │  file_uploads SET                       │
  │    status = REJECTED,                   │
  │    rejectionReason = VIRUS_DETECTED,    │
  │    scannerVerdict = 'macro.exploit.pdf' │
  │    rejectedAt = UTC_NOW                 │
  │  WHERE id = uuid-1234                   │
  └──────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                 │
  ┌──────────────▼──────────────────────────┐
  │  ACTION 3: COMPLETE SERVICE BUS MESSAGE │
  │  message.CompleteAsync()                │
  │  → Stops redelivery                     │
  │  → No other worker picks this up        │
  │  → Pipeline terminates cleanly          │
  └──────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                 │
  ┌──────────────▼──────────────────────────┐
  │  ACTION 4: NOTIFY USER                  │
  │  Email / in-app notification:           │
  │  'Your file report.pdf could not be     │
  │   processed. Our security scanner       │
  │   detected malicious content. The file  │
  │   has been removed. Please contact      │
  │   support if you believe this is an     │
  │   error.'                               │
  │  → No technical details in user message │
  │  → No mention of specific threat name   │
  └──────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                 │
  ┌──────────────▼──────────────────────────┐
  │  ACTION 5: WRITE SECURITY AUDIT LOG     │
  │  Application Insights custom event:     │
  │  {                                      │
  │    event: 'VirusScanRejection',         │
  │    tenantId: 'financecouk',             │
  │    userId: 'u-99',                      │
  │    fileId: 'uuid-1234',                 │
  │    contentHash: 'a3f8c2d1...',          │
  │    scannerVerdict: 'macro.exploit.pdf'  │
  │    detectedAt: timestamp,               │
  │    blobDeletedAt: timestamp             │
  │  }                                      │
  │  → Retained for 90 days minimum         │
  │  → Alerting rule: notify security team  │
  │    if >3 rejections from same tenant    │
  │    in 1 hour (potential attack pattern) │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WHAT MUST NEVER HAPPEN:
  ✗ Content parsing runs on infected file
  ✗ Thumbnail generated from infected file
  ✗ File indexed for search
  ✗ Infected blob URL returned to any client
  ✗ File retained in any storage tier

sections.heading: Key Principles
items: Delete blob before updating any status — deletion makes the file unreachable before any downstream action can reference its path
Do not expose scanner verdict details in user-facing messages — telling a user exactly which exploit was detected helps attackers understand what your scanner catches and what it might miss
Write the audit log even if blob deletion succeeds — security events must be recorded regardless of outcome for compliance and incident response
Alert on repeated rejections from the same tenant — three infected files from the same organisation in an hour is an attack pattern, not bad luck. Automate the escalation
Complete the Service Bus message explicitly on rejection — do not abandon it or let it expire. Abandonment triggers redelivery, which means the same infected file gets processed again

sections.heading: The Scanner Bypass Problem
sections.content:
Virus scanners work by matching file content against known threat signatures. A sufficiently sophisticated attacker can craft a file that passes the scanner on upload but unpacks or activates its payload after extraction or execution.

For DocFlow, the defence is defence in depth — never execute or render uploaded files directly in your application. Parsed content goes into the database as structured data, not as rendered HTML or executed code. Thumbnails are generated in an isolated process with no network access. The scanner is your first line of defence, not your only one.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
pros: Immediate deletion eliminates the attack surface — no window exists where the infected file is reachable after detection
Clean audit trail enables compliance reporting — GDPR, ISO 27001, and SOC 2 all require evidence that security events were detected and handled
Tenant-level alerting catches attack patterns before they escalate — a single infected file is an incident, three in an hour is a breach attempt
cons: Immediate deletion means no forensic copy — if the scanner produces a false positive, the original file is gone. Mitigate by storing the content hash so the user can resubmit and verify
User notification must be carefully worded — too technical and it helps attackers, too vague and it frustrates legitimate users who uploaded a clean file that was incorrectly flagged
Scanner false positives on legitimate documents (complex PDFs, macro-enabled Excel files) will frustrate enterprise users — maintain a scanner tuning process and a support escalation path

idealAnswer.oneLineSummary: An infected file must be deleted before any other action — sequence matters in security response because every step before deletion is a window where malicious content is still reachable in your infrastructure.

steps.interviewerSays: It is 3pm on a Tuesday. A DocFlow enterprise user raises a support ticket — they uploaded a large CSV file at 10am, it has been showing 'Processing' for 5 hours, and nothing has happened. Your team investigates. The worker picked up the job, started content parsing, and then went silent. No error in the logs. No status update. The job is just stuck. How do you detect this class of problem automatically — before users have to raise a support ticket — and how do you design the system to recover from it?
steps.context: This tests production observability and self-healing system design. A 3-5 year engineer who has only worked in development rarely thinks about what happens when a job silently hangs. The right answer introduces job timeout detection, Application Insights alerting, and automatic requeue — three production essentials that never appear in tutorials.

options.text: Add more detailed logging inside the content parsing step — if the worker logs its progress every 10 seconds, the team can see exactly where it got stuck by reading the logs when a user complains
options.interviewerReaction: Better logging is always worthwhile — but it is reactive. You still need a user to complain before anyone looks at the logs. 5 hours passed before this job was noticed. With 3,000 uploads per hour across 180 tenants, how many other jobs are silently stuck right now that no user has complained about yet? How do you make the system tell you when a job is stuck, rather than waiting for a user to discover it?

options.text: Implement a job timeout watchdog — a scheduled Azure Function that runs every 5 minutes, queries the database for any processing job whose status has not changed in more than 15 minutes, marks those jobs as TIMED_OUT, publishes them back to the Service Bus queue for reprocessing, and fires an Application Insights alert with the job details so the team is notified before any user complains
options.interviewerReaction: Exactly right. The watchdog pattern turns a passive database into an active monitor. The 15-minute threshold catches genuinely stuck jobs without false-positiving on legitimately slow ones. Requeueing gives the job a second chance automatically. And the alert means your team knows before the user does — which is the difference between proactive operations and reactive support. What do you check before requeueing to make sure you are not creating an infinite retry loop for a job that will always fail?

options.text: Increase the Service Bus message lock duration to 6 hours — this gives the worker more time to complete long-running jobs without the message being redelivered prematurely, which should prevent jobs from appearing stuck
options.interviewerReaction: A 6-hour message lock means a genuinely crashed worker holds the lock for 6 hours before the message is redelivered. You have not fixed the stuck job — you have just made it invisible for longer. The user still waits 6 hours before automatic recovery begins. The correct approach is to detect that the job is stuck independently of the Service Bus lock, and recover it proactively. How do you know a job is stuck without relying on the message lock to expire?

idealAnswer.summary: Silent failures in async pipelines are only visible through active monitoring — not logs, not user complaints. A job timeout watchdog queries the database for stalled jobs on a regular schedule, requeues them automatically, and alerts the team before any user notices. This is the difference between a system that self-heals and a system that accumulates invisible failures.

sections.heading: Why Silent Failures Are the Hardest Production Problem
sections.content:
A loud failure — an exception, a 500 error, a crashed pod — is easy to detect. It shows up in logs, alerts, and dashboards immediately. A silent failure is different. The worker starts the job, reaches a point where it hangs — a network call that never times out, a database query waiting on a lock, an infinite loop in a parsing edge case — and just stops producing output. No exception. No error. Just silence.

Without active monitoring, silent failures are invisible until a user complains. At DocFlow's scale of 3,000 uploads per hour, even a 0.1% silent failure rate means 3 stuck jobs every hour. Over a business day, that is 24 stuck jobs that users are waiting on — each one a support ticket, a trust erosion event, a churn risk.

The watchdog pattern solves this by treating the database as the source of truth for job health. If a job's status has not changed in longer than the maximum expected processing time, the job is stuck — regardless of what the worker thinks it is doing.

sections.heading: Job Timeout Watchdog Architecture
sections.content:
Azure Function (Timer Trigger — every 5 minutes)
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
  WatchdogFunction runs:
               │
               ▼
  STEP 1: FIND STALLED JOBS
  SELECT * FROM file_processing_jobs
  WHERE status IN ('SCANNING','PARSING','PROCESSING')
  AND   lastUpdatedAt < DATEADD(MINUTE,-15,GETUTCDATE())
  AND   retryCount < 3
               │
               ▼
  STEP 2: FOR EACH STALLED JOB
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Update DB:                             │
  │    status = TIMED_OUT                   │
  │    timedOutAt = UTC_NOW                 │
  │    retryCount = retryCount + 1          │
  │                                         │
  │  Publish to Service Bus:                │
  │    queue: file-processing-jobs          │
  │    message: {                           │
  │      fileId: uuid-1234,                 │
  │      isRetry: true,                     │
  │      retryCount: 2,                     │
  │      originalStartedAt: ...             │
  │    }                                    │
  │                                         │
  │  Update DB:                             │
  │    status = QUEUED (requeued)           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘
               │
               ▼
  STEP 3: ALERT IF STALLED JOBS FOUND
  Application Insights custom event:
  {
    event: 'StalledJobsDetected',
    count: 3,
    jobs: [uuid-1234, uuid-5678, uuid-9012],
    oldestStalledAt: '10:03am',
    detectedAt: '3:05pm'
  }
  Alert rule: fire PagerDuty if count > 5
  in a single watchdog run
               │
               ▼
  STEP 4: HANDLE EXHAUSTED RETRIES
  SELECT * FROM file_processing_jobs
  WHERE status = 'TIMED_OUT'
  AND   retryCount >= 3
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  → Update status: FAILED_PERMANENT
  → Notify user: 'Processing failed after
    multiple attempts. Please re-upload.'
  → Alert engineering team with full
    job context for investigation
  → Do NOT requeue — infinite loop risk

  STATUS LIFECYCLE:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  PENDING_UPLOAD
       │
  QUEUED ◄──────────────────── TIMED_OUT
       │                            ▲
  SCANNING ──── (no update 15min) ──┘
       │
  PARSING  ──── (no update 15min) ──┐
       │                            │
  PROCESSING ─ (no update 15min) ───┘
       │
  COMPLETE / REJECTED / FAILED_PERMANENT

sections.heading: Key Principles
items: The watchdog threshold (15 minutes) must be longer than the maximum legitimate processing time — if your slowest job takes 10 minutes, set the threshold to 15. Too short and you requeue jobs that are still running
retryCount is your infinite loop protection — without it, a job that always hangs at the same point gets requeued forever. Three retries is a reasonable default before declaring permanent failure
Update status to TIMED_OUT before requeueing — if the watchdog crashes between the requeue and the status update, you have a duplicate job in the queue. Update first, then enqueue
lastUpdatedAt must be updated at the start of each processing step, not just at completion — this is what the watchdog reads. A step that takes 20 minutes must emit a heartbeat update partway through
Alert threshold should be count-based, not binary — one stalled job might be a one-off. Five in a single watchdog run suggests a systemic problem: worker crash, dependency outage, or a bad deployment

sections.heading: The Heartbeat Problem for Long Steps
sections.content:
Content parsing of a 500MB CSV file might legitimately take 12 minutes. If your watchdog fires after 15 minutes of no status change, it will incorrectly mark a healthy long-running job as stalled and requeue it — now two workers are parsing the same file simultaneously.

The fix: introduce a heartbeat update. Every 2 minutes during a long-running step, the worker writes a progress update to the database — not a status change, just a timestamp and a progress percentage. The watchdog checks lastHeartbeatAt instead of lastUpdatedAt. A job that is actively making progress keeps its heartbeat current and never triggers the watchdog. A job that is genuinely stuck stops sending heartbeats and gets detected.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
pros: Stalled jobs are detected and recovered automatically — users never wait more than 20 minutes before the system self-heals
Team is alerted before users complain — proactive operations instead of reactive support
Permanent failure after three retries prevents infinite retry loops for jobs that will always fail at the same point
Heartbeat pattern distinguishes genuinely stuck jobs from legitimately slow ones — no false positives on large file processing
cons: Workers must implement heartbeat emission — adds code to every long-running step. Easy to forget in a new step, creating a false stall signal
Watchdog is another service to deploy, monitor, and maintain — timer trigger functions can themselves fail silently if not monitored

Retry requeue means the same job may be processed by a different worker with a different environment — if the failure is environment-specific (a missing dependency on one worker pod), retry on a different pod may succeed or may obscure a real infrastructure problem

idealAnswer.oneLineSummary: Silent failures in async pipelines are invisible until a user complains — a job timeout watchdog queries the database for stalled jobs, requeues them automatically, and alerts your team proactively, turning invisible failures into observable, recoverable events.

bands.label: Production-Ready Engineer
bands.message: You demonstrated strong systems thinking across all five problems — presigned URL architecture, async pipeline design, idempotency, security-first incident response, and proactive observability. These are the patterns that separate engineers who build reliable systems from engineers who build systems that work in development but fail silently in production.

bands.label: Good Foundation, Production Gaps
bands.message: Solid instincts on the architecture fundamentals but gaps in production reliability thinking. Focus on idempotency design, security response sequencing, and active job monitoring. These topics come up in every senior engineering interview and every production post-mortem.

bands.label: Core Concepts to Strengthen
bands.message: Revisit presigned URL upload patterns, async job queue architecture with status tracking, idempotency in distributed systems, and production observability with watchdog patterns. Build a small file processing pipeline as a side project — these concepts click much faster when you have implemented them once end to end.

sections.heading: Idempotency - Simply Explained
sections.content:
Think about a lift button. You press the button to call the lift. It lights up. Now you press it again. And again. And again — because the lift is taking too long. What happens? Nothing extra. The lift still comes once. Pressing the button ten times produces exactly the same result as pressing it once. One lift. One arrival. No matter how many times you pressed.

That is idempotency. An operation that can be performed multiple times and always produces the same result as if it was performed once. No extra side effects. No duplicate outcomes. Press ten times, get one lift.

Now think about why this matters in software. Your application sends a request to a server — place this order, process this payment, create this user. The server receives the request, processes it, and just as it is about to send the response back — the network drops. Your application never receives the response. It has no idea if the request succeeded or failed. So it does the only sensible thing. It tries again.

Here is the problem. If your server is not idempotent, that retry just created a second order. Charged the customer twice. Created two user accounts. The original request succeeded — the customer just never found out. The retry then succeeded again. Now you have a very angry customer and a very embarrassing support ticket.

An idempotent server handles this gracefully. When the retry arrives, the server recognises it as a duplicate of a request it already processed. It does not process it again. It simply returns the same response as the first time. One order. One charge. One user account. Regardless of how many times the client retried.

The way this is implemented is straightforward. The client generates a unique ID for each request — called an idempotency key — before sending it. Something like a UUID. It sends this key along with the request. The server stores the key and the result of processing that request. When the retry arrives with the same key, the server looks it up, finds it has already been processed, and returns the stored result without doing anything twice.

The operations you use every day are already designed around this. GET requests are idempotent — asking for a webpage ten times returns the same webpage ten times, nothing changes on the server. DELETE requests are idempotent — deleting something that is already deleted simply returns success, nothing explodes. POST requests are not idempotent by default — submitting a form ten times creates ten records. Making POST requests idempotent is your responsibility as the engineer, and idempotency keys are how you do it.

Idempotency is not a nice-to-have. In a world where networks drop, servers restart, and clients retry — and they always do — an API without idempotency is an API that silently corrupts data under pressure. You will never see the problem in development. You will absolutely see it in production, at three in the morning, when a customer has been charged six times for one order.
